13891: The diversion of flow from rivers can impose unfavourable conditions for fishes, including accelerating seasonal water quality deterioration. As part of local water security measures for the Australian Capital Territory (ACT), a pipeline is being constructed that will divert water from the Murrumbidgee River to Googong Reservoir (M2G). Flow diversions through the pipeline could negatively affect upland populations of the iconic and nationally threatened Murray cod Maccullochella peelii peelii occurring in downstream river reaches. "Protected" flows for Murray cod have been proposed to guide M2G pipeline operation based on flow requirements of the species, however spawning and larval ecology in upland environments is unknown. The way in which flow influences adverse water quality conditions is also not fully understood in the affected reaches of the Murrumbidgee River. A study has commenced to determine the spatial and temporal nature of Murray cod breeding as well as the relationships between dissolved oxygen, temperature and flow in the affected Murrumbidgee River reaches. Preliminary results suggest larvae drift from November to mid December, and spawning occurs as far upstream as Tharwa near the M2G pipeline. Episodes of low dissolved oxygen were observed over summer 2011/12 when high rainfall and cooler than historic temperatures occurred. These conditions are likely exacerbated under warmer climatic scenarios and reduced flow. Continued research will facilitate the development of flow dependent ecological requirements for upland Murray cod; an approach that will assist management and conservation of freshwater fishes in highly regulated river systems, including those of the Murray-Darling Basin.

13892: Market sampling for Snapper has identified considerable differences in the size structures amongst different regions of South Australia's fishery. The aim of the Honours study was to determine whether this reflected spatial variation in growth, and possible influences of diet on growth. Commercial market sampling provided samples of Snapper from four regions, Northern Spencer Gulf (NSG), Southern Spencer Gulf (SSG), Northern Gulf St. Vincent (NGSV) and Southern Gulf St. Vincent (SGSV). Snapper grew faster in the northern gulfs than in the southern gulfs. Furthermore, diet differed significantly amongst regions. In NSG, Blue Swimmer Crabs were the dominant prey, in NGSV Blue Swimmer Crabs, the mussel Modiolus aerolatus and Red Swimmer Crabs were the dominant prey species. The percentage of snapper containing food and Gut Fullness Index (GF) were higher in the northern gulfs, particularly NGSV. Significant seasonal and ontogenetic differences in diet and food consumption for each region were also found. It was concluded that these taxonomic differences in the diets and amounts of food consumed were likely to have contributed to the observed regional differences in growth characteristics.

13893: Recreational fishers have a long history of gillnet usage in Tasmania, targeting species that traditionally have been difficult to catch using angling methods, species such as bastard trumpeter, blue warehou, flounder and mullet. The present study provides a comprehensive assessment of the status of recreational gillnetting in Tasmania, including the impacts of management measures that have been progressively introduced since the late 1990s to improve fishing practices. The most significant of these has been the prohibition of night netting in most regions. This measure has not only resulted in a marked reduction in the proportion of night sets (from 75% of the state-wide effort in 1997 to 8% in 2010) but also a substantial reduction in overall recreational netting effort. For instance, recreational gillnet effort (net-days) in 2010 was about 60% of that in 1997, despite 40% more registered gillnet licence-holders in 2010. Several characteristics of the recreational gillnet fishery have, however, remained consistent through time, including the relative distribution of effort around the state and the main species targeted and caught. The most conspicuous changes in catch composition appear to be a decline in the importance of flounder as a gillnet species, influenced by the restriction on night netting, and the increasing importance of Atlantic salmon escapees as a target species, linked to the expansion of the salmonid industry in Tasmania.

13895: Live food supply is a key factor contributing to the success of larval fish rearing. This study was divided into two feeding phases: rotifer feeding from 3-14 DPH (phase I), and Artemia nauplii feeding from 15-22 DPH (phase II). In phase I, four rotifer densities (1, 10, 20, and 40/ml) were used. In phase II, Artemia started at 0.8 nauplii/ml on 15 DPH, and then the density of Artemia was daily incremented at 50%, 70%, 90% and 110% respectively in four treatments from 15 to 22 DPH. In phase I, rotifer density significantly affected larval growth, but not survival. After 5 DPH, the number of rotifers consumed by fish did not differ between rotifer densities. In phase II, both fish growth and survival were affected by Artemia densities, but the amount of Artemia consumed by fish significantly differ between prey densities. The result suggests that rotifer densities be offered at 20-40/ml before 6 DPH, and 10-20/ml afterwards to support fish growth and survival. Likewise, Artemia is recommended at a daily increment of 90-110% of 0.8/ml from 15 to 22 DPH. This study proposes a management protocol to use appropriate type and quantity of live food to feed yellowtail kingfish larvae, which could be applicable to larval culture of other marine fish species.

13896: Defining the ecological impacts conferred by invasive fishes provides a framework for evaluating the feasibility of control efforts in invaded waterways, and for predicting the consequences of future incursions. Eastern gambusia (Gambusia holbrooki) is a remarkably successful invader of freshwater systems worldwide, with the capacity to detrimentally impact native fishes both directly (e.g. competition, predation, agonistic interactions) and indirectly (e.g. triggering trophic cascades). Here, we modelled the influence of eastern gambusia and several environmental covariates on fish species diversity, abundance and condition based on quantitative survey data collected from 93 wetlands in south-eastern Australia. We predicted that small-bodied, wetland specialist species sharing dietary- and habitat-niches with eastern gambusia would be most severely impacted, and that environmental stressors associated with wetland drying during late summer would magnify these impacts. Eastern gambusia influenced the occurrence, abundance and/or body condition of most common wetland species; however, the direction and level of impact appeared dependent upon both biotic and environmental forces. From these results, we postulate that generalist life-history strategies that permit niche-segregation may release some native species from competitive/predatory pressures, allowing coexistence with eastern gambusia in resource-limited, environmentally harsh habitats, whilst specialist species that occupy narrower ecological niches may be less resistant.

13897: The decline of black cod Epinephelus daemelii, a subtropical southwest Pacific endemic, led to their protection in 1983 in NSW. They are presently classified as vulnerable in Australia. 13898: In southern Australia, gummy shark and southern fiddler ray are commonly captured by recreational and commercial fisheries. 13899: Kangaroo Island's Middle River is the only impounded river on a largely unchanged island. The river is home to three fish species, all of which have the capacity for diadromous life cycles. 13900: Abalone exhibit fine-scale population structure because the larvae are not widely dispersed and adults are sedentary. These populations also typically have variable life-history parameters that influence population size-structure, size-at maturity and productivity. The increased recognition of spatially-complex stock structures now requires the current broad-scale management approach to be modified such that fishery management is more closely aligned with the component populations. Since 2004, this vexing problem has been addressed for blacklip abalone in the Southern Zone of the South Australian fishery, where this species comprises local-scale mosaics of fast (termed 'non-stunted') and slower (termed 'stunted') growing populations. A morphometric marker, based on the ratio between shell length and shell height, was identified to distinguish between 'stunted' and 'non-stunted' abalone and predict key biological variables including size-at-maturity, growth rate and fecundity. Using shells from commercial catch sampling, this provided a tool for distinguishing among blacklip populations and determining appropriate minimum legal sizes. However, implementation was hindered by the difficulties of (1) establishing a cost-effective, but robust, fishery compliance system and (2) setting appropriate catch limits for each population. These issues have recently been overcome through trialling alternative compliance tools including vessel monitoring systems and finalisation of the harvest strategy for the fishery. Consequently, fine-scale, spatial management of this fishery is now a key priority for PIRSA Fisheries & Aquaculture, the management agency. This paper describes the application of biological and fishery data to restructuring the fishery, identifies the process underway and speculates on the management structure of the Southern Zone following implementation.

13901: Sturgeons are a precious and endangered species in Iran, which are harvested commercially for caviar and flesh. Stocking of fingerlings is undertaken to enhance commercial fishing opportunities and aid recovery of the species. When first stocked, fish are exposed to salinity shock as freshwater-reared fish are released into estuaries. This study was performed to examine physiological responses (size and number of chloride cells, level of cortisol in blood plasma) of exposure to different concentrations of hydrocortisone, which prepares fingerlings for release into brackish water. Fishes were treated by bathing with three different hydrocortisone sodium phosphate (hereafter hormone) concentrations (3, 5 and 7 ppm). Gill tissues were also incubated in an in vitro test. Blood cortisol levels along with changes in the size and numbers of gill chloride cells were measured after exposure. 13902: The Rivers of the Lake Eyre Basin are some of the last unregulated waters in Australia. SARDI research under the Neales River and Cooper Creek Critical Refugia projects, and the Lake Eyre Basin Rivers Assessment (LEBRA) has provided continuous and broad-scale data on the flux of fish populations in this environment. Hydrology in the basin is variable and climate driven, with wetting and drying regimes occurring at seasonal and decadal scales. The presence of natural flow regimes enables the assessment of species' interaction with climatic cycles to drive the expansion and contraction of fish assemblages in line with patterns of hydrological connectivity. During periods of increasing hydrological connectivity, it is predicted that more resilient fish species will move quickly into new habitats before less resilient species. Periods of declining rainfall, will maintain more resistant species' populations within environmentally harsh habitats (e.g. hypersaline pools) while less resistant species will decline. It is possible that natural hydrological regimes have led to a highly resilient native fish population. In conjunction with the impacts of hydrological regime, this may provide a challenge to the establishment of introduced aquatic biota. Following drought conditions in the mid 2000s, fish recolonised catchments to establish populations in previously dry waterholes. Recolonisation responses were species-specific following predictable resilience patterns based on trait. Populations colonised previously dry ephemeral catchments from connected neighbouring rivers along obvious dispersal routes (e.g. Warburton-Macumba) whilst isolating mechanisms maintained discrete populations in rivers such as the Finke River. Patterns of connectivity between some rivers remain unresolved, but work is underway through LEBRA and the National Climate Change Adaptation Facility (NCCARF) to address the relationships across Lake Eyre Basin fish populations using several techniques including tagging, genetics, and otolith microchemistry.

13903: Adult fish stocks are highly dependent on the recruitment success of juveniles at the nursery grounds. All fish species were collected using seine nets with a 1-mm mesh along with concurrent sampling of both pelagic and benthic potential food resources. 13904: It is well known that when you deploy artificial structures on soft sediments in the marine environment you get an increase in the diversity and abundance of fish at a location. 13905: The past half century has seen substantial changes in native freshwater fish abundance and species assemblages. Among the many tools available to resource management and conservation agencies to respond to such change, population and evolutionary genetics remain useful in guiding management responses. Genetic tools have been valuable in the development of captive breeding and stocking protocols, hatchery quality assurance programs, and translocation policies. Genetics has been used to guide fish rescue efforts when dealing with catastrophic events during the recent drought such as bushfires and the drying of waterways. Genetic tools have also guided the reestablishment and rebuilding of these populations and continue to play an important role in species recovery planning. These tools can identify which species are more likely to become imperilled and help predict adaptive potential and population resilience. Genetics can also provide insights into the colonisation of exotic species within Australia.

13906: Pairs of closely related species on either side of a barrier provide an opportunity to test evolutionary hypotheses. In southern Australian seas, many species pairs occur on either side of the Bass Strait, which temporarily becomes an isthmus during glacial stages. We used mitochondrial and nuclear approaches to examine recent demographic changes in one such species pair, Arripis trutta (east of Bass Strait) and A. truttaceus (west of Bass Strait). Data from the two remaining members of the family Arripidae, A. xylabion and A. georgianus, were included to provide context for interpreting patterns in the focal species pair. All Arripis species were characterised by low genetic diversity and there was evidence for a more recent and/or severe population contraction in A. truttaceus compared to A. trutta. These different demographic signals support the a priori hypothesis that environmental conditions to the west of the Bass Strait were more severe than to the east during glacial stages and, in particular, the last glacial maximum. The results are considered in the context of the biology of the species and the historical marine biogeography of temperate Australia.

13907: Hybridisation was recently discovered along the eastern Australian coastline between the globally distributed common blacktip shark, Carcharhinus limbatus, and the morphologically similar endemic Australian blacktip shark, C. tilstoni. The two species dominate the catch of commercial shark fisheries across northern Australia. They are closely related but grow to different maximum sizes, have different numbers of vertebrae and are genetically distinct. Using seven nuclear DNA markers in addition to mitochondrial DNA we now show that hybrids can be identified in the absence of morphological information. Additional screening of animals caught off Western Australia and the Northern Territory extends the hybrid zone across northern Australia. There is some evidence of a spatial component to the frequency and direction of hybridization which is probably driven by differences in local frequencies of parental species. Although hybrid animals have been found at all sampling locations, first generation (F1) hybrids are rare. The absence of F1 hybrids indicates that hybridization has successfully mixed the species in the past but that modern day crosses are possibly infrequent or might produce offspring with lower fitness. This may explain why pure parental species are still the most common animals caught. Sustainable management of this species complex requires more information on stock boundaries and the relative impact of hybridization.

13908: Good models rely on good data. In a climate change context, good data can take the form of the historical record: by observing how biology has responded to past climatic variability, we can gain insights into how it will respond to future environmental conditions. Long-term biological datasets are relatively common for terrestrial taxa and environments, but extremely sparse for aquatic systems. Aquatic biochronologies, generated from time-dependent information recorded in fish otoliths (ear stones) that are archived in their millions worldwide, can provide valuable long-term ecological insights into marine and freshwater environments. This resource is, however, currently under-utilised in the measurement and prediction of ecological responses to climate change, despite its potential to provide unprecedented levels of spatial and temporal detail in aquatic environments. We generated six, 30-year long, otolith biochronologies for tiger flathead (Platycephalus richardsoni) from across their range in south east Australia and related estimates of inter-annual growth variability to environmental and population abundance parameters. Growth rates in all populations increased through time and were related to the oceanic temperature increases observed throughout this region. We hypothesise warming, especially for southerly populations, has resulted in conditions more favourable to metabolic performance and thus increased growth rates. The effect of population abundance on growth rates differed among chronologies and may reflect spatial and temporal differences in commercial fishing pressure. Our results indicate that projected ocean temperature rises will result in spatially differentiated changes in tiger flathead stock productivity and a possible northerly range contraction.

13909: Fisheries managers need the latest social, economic and biological data to support decision-making about harvesting that is both sustainable and profitable. Stakeholders were canvassed to identify the most important issues in fisheries management, and here we show that genetics provides useful outcomes for seven of the eleven most important issues. This talk provides specific examples of how genetic technologies can address particular management themes. We describe and evaluate linkages between management and genetics by scoring the relative cost, readiness, utility and maturity of genetic technologies to address various management themes. The links between management and genetic themes are summarised in a 'look-up' table that allows managers and scientists to understand which genetic technology is useful and why, and allows fisheries geneticists to understand the management context for their research. 13912: Climate driven changes in the distribution of marine species are being reported from around the globe, however, the rate of range extension or contraction varies in both space and time. To minimise negative impacts and maximise opportunities, we need monitoring infrastructure in place to capture distributional changes within reasonable time frames and with a degree of certainty. Redmap (Range Extension Database and Mapping project, www.redmap.org.au) is an online database and mapping resource allowing members of the public to submit observational data (including photographs) of marine species occurring outside their known distribution (i.e. species that may be undergoing range shifts). A successful pilot in Tasmania is expanding to an Australian-wide long-term biodiversity monitoring system (launching October 2012), designed to be a low-cost and sustained approach to assess changing marine species distributions. Australia has over 3.5 million fishers and divers - many equipped with consumer electronics and the capacity to record verifiable observations. However, one challenge to the adoption of such datasets is the perception of bias or low quality. In addition to extracting geo-tag information from photographs (validating location), species identifications are verified by essentially 'crowd-sourcing' from a large panel of expert scientists using a semi-automated validation workflow. This initiative has the potential to generate large amounts of valuable information for researchers and engage communities in climate science (using their own data), raising awareness of climate change impacts and consequences. Redmap is an early warning system for changes occurring in the marine environment, and has the potential to play a pivotal role in directing management decisions and actions.

13913: Population models using mark-resight methods are becoming widely used for assessing the population size and abundance trends of marine species. 13916: Estuaries provide putative nursery areas for many marine migrant species and play a fundamental role in supporting coastal stocks. 13917: Aerial surveys are a recognised technique to identify the presence and abundance of marine animals. 13918: The Australian Lungfish (Neoceratodus forsteri) is a declared threatened species, at risk from anthropogenic impacts. 13919: Preliminary analysis of available data indicate the periods of embryonic growth (12-15 months) and ovarian cycle are synchronous and seasonal among breeding females across the population. 13920: The school shark (Galeorhinus galeus) is a long-lived, migratory carcharhinid that has been the focus of considerable fisheries research in the Australasian region. 13921: The South Australian reach of Cooper Creek is a high ecological value environment at the downstream end of a largely unregulated river system. 13922: Whale sharks occur in the three major oceans spanning the equator and are observed, even if only occasionally, near the shore of over 100 countries. The connectivity of the individuals frequenting these locations is still poorly understood given a paucity of data and technology to survey entire ocean basins. We tested the hypothesis that whale shark occurrence in different ocean basins is a function of similar environmental predictors. We used opportunistically logged data of whale shark sightings derived from tuna purse-seine fisheries to validate our predictions and results show good agreement with known occurrences. We found that depth and sea surface temperature are the major drivers of whale shark occurrence, and that habitat suitability varies seasonally among the three ocean basins. Our work is the first to predict and validate whale shark occurrence at an oceanic scale, providing information essential to formulate models of global connectivity. 13923: Flow regulation through a series of barrages resulted in fragmented and environmentally distinct habitats threatening the health of the Murray River estuary. 13924: In WA, Australian herring (Arripis georgianus) has historically been the most common species in the recreational finfish catch and also a significant commercial target species. 13925: Ecosystem-based Fisheries Management (EBFM) is a powerful methodology for maintaining healthy and functioning marine ecosystems. Whole-of-system models such as Atlantis enable us to simulate ecosystem-level impacts of alternative fisheries management regimes and climate effects, and highlight the trade-offs of any candidate strategy with respect to management objectives. In a complex and multi-use system, these simulations can guide the selection of robust management strategies. Managers in the southern Benguela region are international leaders in both implementation of EBFM and in ecosystem modelling to support it. In the context of a complex ecosystem, models which look at fish stocks at an ecosystem level (rather than single species under fishing pressure) are appropriate for exploring the effects of long-term ecosystem changes in a way that provides realistic outputs for management. We also aim to explore the system-level impacts of implementing several single-species management plans in parallel.

13926: Size and growth during the early life history phases of fishes are critical to recruitment success of fish populations, but quantifying such traits can be problematic due to the small size, fragility and limited existence of larvae in time and space. 13927: The exploitation of South Australia's Southern Garfish fishery has historically been high, with annual harvest fractions consistently exceeding 65%, which is approximately double the international standard of 32%. Although the fishery has demonstrated some resilience to this sustained pressure, overall catches and catch rates have steadily declined since 2000/01. Given these concerns, industry members and fishery managers are now focused on developing strategies that will reduce the harvest fraction to <30% by 2020 and promote stock rebuilding. Regulating fishing gear and/or reducing effort are two clear management strategies that will contribute to lowering the exploitation rate to an acceptable level. A variety of management scenarios are currently being considered and tailored specifically towards the hauling net sector of the fishery as this sector accounts for most (~90%) of the State-wide commercial catch. 13929: Yellowtail kingfish (YTK, Seriola lalandi) is a temperate, carnivorous, marine fish species that is widely distributed throughout the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans. 13931: Many fishes make frequent ascents to surface waters and often show prolonged surface swimming following descents to deep water. 13936: Auto-correlation is a widely recognised problem associated with using acoustic telemetry data to analyse the movements of fish. Auto-correlation violates the assumption of data independence and can lead to the F and t-statistics produced using regression analysis providing spurious results. A host of approaches to this problem have been developed including ignoring it altogether. A number of environmental variables were tested against fish location including temperature, salinity and river flow. The best fitting and most parsimonious model was a second order autoregressive model that contained only salinity and two Boolean explanatory variables representing high river discharge events and low water temperature days. The salinity and high river discharge variables were associated with large-scale movements influenced by freshwater inflow events and resultant reductions in salinity levels. The low temperature variable was a substitute for seasonal movement associated with the timing of annual M. colonorum spawning behaviour. A number of variables that were included in the best non-autoregressive model were removed in the best autoregressive model. These results demonstrate the importance of accounting for autocorrelation in telemetry data when evaluating the effect of environmental variables on fish movements.

13937: The occurrence of embryonic diapause (suspension of development at any stage of embryogenesis) is widespread among species from unrelated taxa in all vertebrate groups, including elasmobranchs. There is evidence indicating that at least 14 species of rays and two sharks belonging to 4 orders and 7 families undergo embryonic diapause, suggesting that this form of reproduction exists within a wide range of elasmobranch reproductive modes, including lecithotrophs and matrotrophs. Since the occurrence of such a trait within each taxa is not universal, it is suggested that this form of reproduction has evolved independently in each group. Where it has been investigated, embryogenesis is arrested from four to 10 months, during which the uterine eggs are preserved at the blastodisc stage. The maintenance of diapause has not been investigated but, as in other vertebrates, it possibly involves hormones and environmental cues. The possible control mechanisms will be discussed.

13938: An industry Code of Practice (CoP) has successfully mitigated the operational interactions of the South Australian Sardine Fishery (SASF) with the short-beaked common dolphin (Delphinus delphis). For example, rates of dolphin encirclement recorded by observers fell from 178 dolphins per hundred net-sets in 2004-05 to 43 dolphins per hundred net-sets 2010-11. Similarly, observed mortality rates fell from 39 per hundred net-sets in 2004-05 to 2 dolphins per hundred net-sets in 2010-11. The CoP includes: mandatory crew inductions into mitigation procedures; vessel-specific CoP interaction response flowcharts; bi-monthly skippers meetings to assess the performance of the CoP; quarterly meetings of a Working Group, that includes representatives of Primary Industries and Regions South Australia (PIRSA), Fisheries and Aquaculture, the South Australian Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) and the South Australian Research and Development Institute (SARDI), to monitor interaction rates and assess the need for refinement of the CoP; and formal, annual, independent, public reporting. The efficacy of the CoP in mitigating the interactions with short-beaked common dolphins can be attributed to: i) the success of the avoidance procedures; and ii) the reduced response times and highly successful release procedure (opening the front of the net). In 2010-11, one issue related to the SASF's interactions with the short-beaked common dolphin remained unresolved. Specifically, the rates of encirclement and mortality recorded by observers were 4.5 and 4.4 times higher, respectively, than those recorded in logbooks when an observer was not onboard. To address this discrepancy, the SASF industry in conjunction with SARDI, and with the endorsement of PIRSA and DENR, introduced an industry-based program for real-time monitoring of interactions in 2011-12. This talk documents the success of this program in reducing the discrepancy between observer and logbook data. 13939: The use of genetic tools in fisheries management has been occurring for over 50 years. During this time both fisheries management practices and genetic technology have changed significantly. Given these rapid changes it is important that research and development initiatives are targeted towards the appropriate and up-to-date use of genetic tools to maximise management outcomes. One of the key ingredients to the success of R&D investment into genetics is the support of all fisheries stakeholders. To better understand the views of stakeholders about the use of genetic tools in fisheries management we conducted interviews with different fisheries stakeholder groups within Australia and internationally. These included fisheries scientists, geneticists, fisheries managers and industry representatives. The interview questions asked about stakeholder awareness/knowledge of genetic methods and applications, perceptions about the use of genetics in fisheries, communication between geneticists and stakeholders, and future management issues. During the interviews we found that poor communication between geneticists and other stakeholders hindered the uptake of genetic research in fisheries, and identified ways to improve this. We also identified and ranked the importance of key management issues based on the feedback from interviewees. In this talk we present the results of these interviews which provide a unique insight into perceptions that can help improve not only the future use of genetics in fisheries, but also the future interface between science and fisheries management more generally.

13940: Understanding the size-specific selectivity of fishing gears is critical to the proper assessment of harvested fish stocks. Combined with information on growth, fecundity, and mortality, parameters describing size-specific selectivity can be used to determine strategies for optimizing yield from a fishery. Current standard procedures for estimating selectivity parameters from catch data are well established, but do not allow for the estimation of parameters to describe non-replicating selective agents such as piscivorous birds. This study developed a method to allow for the simultaneous estimation of selectivity parameters from multiple fishing gears, and thus for the estimation of non-replicating selectivity parameters in conjunction with replicating parameters that describe trawl nets, gillnets or hooks. Such methods can be generalised and used to estimate the parameters of other fishing agents, such as abalone divers, and do not rely, like other methods, on assumptions concerning fishing power. The methods developed in this study are available for general application in the form of R scripts, and can be applied to multiple data types from a wide variety of fisheries.

13941: It is important to understand how an animal moves and interacts with this changing environment. In south-eastern Australia, estuaries have been experiencing extreme drought with further periods of extended drought and extreme flooding predicted for the future. In this study we used modern acoustic telemetry technology to investigate patterns of movement in two estuarine species in two drought-affected estuaries. We tagged 41 black bream Acanthopagrus butcheri and 25 estuary perch Macquaria colonorum in the Mitchell and Tambo Rivers in south-eastern Australia. We placed 12 acoustic receivers in the Mitchell River and 9 in the Tambo River at 2 km intervals. A Bayesian state-space model gave us high detection probabilities for both species at all receivers. Black bream were highly mobile, regularly moving up and down the estuary and into the lakes and neighbouring rivers. Movement rates were very similar between both rivers. Compared to estuary perch which had a very small home range and made occasional short upstream or downstream movements. Interestingly, estuary perch move at greater rates in the Tambo River when compared to fish in the Mitchell. A GLM revealed that freshwater flow, moon phase and season had significant effects on the position of fish and the home range of fish. The timing of large flow events, in particularly in spring during the spawning season, could have a significant effect on annual spawning success. As both these species displayed significantly different use of the estuary, this needs to be taken into consideration in future conservation and management of these species.

13942: Sustainable fisheries management and resource allocation between fishing sectors require estimates of recreational fishing from surveys that require representative samples from the target population. 13943: Lindsay-Mulcra-Wallpolla Islands (LMW) is a floodplain anabranch system of the Murray River located in the north-west corner of Victoria. Fish monitoring across LMW has been conducted annually as part of the Living Murray Project since 2006. Annual monitoring can provide information on long-term trends in fish communities. After approximately 10 years of low/regulated Murray River flows, natural flooding of the Murray River occurred in 2010-11. This trend was driven by comparatively high numbers of non-native species (89.7% of total catch), in particular Eastern Gambusia and Common Carp, which were far more abundant than pre-flood surveys. Post-flooding survey, however demonstrated a decline in species diversity (17 to 14 species) and total abundance (n=27 605 to n=7 865). Post flood abundance of Common Carp was greater than both pre and during flood surveys, while the abundance of Eastern Gambusia was reduced compared with all previous surveys. The abundances of small-bodied native fish were generally lower during flood surveys than pre and post-flood surveys. Conversely, Murray Cod abundance was reduced during and post-flood surveys compared with pre-flood surveys, which may reflect catchability of this species during high flows.

13944: Swimbladder inflation largely determines buoyancy and vertical movement of larvae in early life. Mortality usually occurs in fish where swimbladder inflation fails. The ontogeny of larval body density and the morphological events during swimbladder development were investigated in yellowtail kingfish Seriola lalandi (YTK) to understand the functional relationship between larval morphology and body density. Histological evidence demonstrates YTK larvae are initially transient physostomes, with the inflation window occurring between 3 and 5 days post hatch. Initial inflation of the swimbladder occurs through a pneumatic duct, and larvae develop as physoclistous adults with the formation of the rete mirabile. Swimbladder inflation had a direct effect on larval body density. During the early developmental stage, larvae without swimbladder inflation became negatively buoyant and their body density gradually increased above the surrounding environment. These larvae are prone to sinking death syndrome during the night-phase when larvae have reduced swimming behaviour thus larvae sink to the tank bottoms leading to high mortalities. The effect of abiotic factors such light, temperature and oxygen supersaturation on swimbladder inflation rates were investigated. Swimbladder inflation was significantly improved under artificial light with a high light intensity (>30 000 lux). Temperature and oxygen supersaturation during early YTK larvae rearing did not significantly improve swimbladder inflation however growth was impacted by the rearing temperature.

13945: Effective management of shark populations requires detailed understanding of essential habitats and how these habitats are utilised by sharks. Coastal embayments along the central Great Barrier Reef coast provide important nursery habitat for young sharks. However, how young sharks utilise these waters remains poorly understood, especially across larger geographic scales. Further, the importance of nursery habitat diversity along this environmentally heterogeneous coastal stretch remains un-quantified. Portfolio theory suggests that the utilisation of a diverse range of nursery habitats may reduce variability in the overall productivity of juveniles across a region and improve the adaptability of a species to environmental change. Fishery independent surveys were undertaken to investigate juvenile shark biodiversity and abundance along the central Great Barrier Reef coast between Cardwell and Proserpine. Preliminary findings indicate spatial variability in how these waters are utilised by young sharks, and highlight the environmental factors that may drive these variations. 13946: The Coorong is the unique estuary of the Murray-Darling Basin, located at the terminus of the Murray-Darling River. Freshwater flow plays a pivotal role in maintaining estuarine habitat and functionality and affecting aquatic biota. The present study investigated spatio-temporal variation in fish assemblage structure and distribution, abundance and recruitment of key species along the Murray estuary, North and South lagoons of the Coorong during recent drought and flood years (2006/07 - 2011/12). Consequently, fish assemblage composition changed; species richness, diversity and abundance increased. Smallmouth hardyhead (Atherinosoma microstoma) recolonised the South Lagoon with a dramatic increase in abundance following salinity reductions to <100‰. 13947: We wanted to track the movements of New Zealand rig (Mustelus lenticulatus) within an estuarine spawning site to understand rig habitat use, mating dynamics, and tidal, diurnal and feeding behaviour. Within a localised area, such as an estuary or harbour, our method uses a mesh network of low-powered digital radios to transmit, receive and deliver any data collected by mobile environmental sensors or GPS locators. In our case, the GPS tags were designed to be mounted in a float that is tethered to an adult rig. Digi International produces a family of small (22 x 32 mm), light (only 4 g), and low-cost (AUS$ 52) wireless communication modules (called XBee's) that use low power (3.3V @ 215mA) and can transmit over 1600 m (line-of-sight range). By using one XBee as a network coordinator, one or more as the mobile data-originating devices (end-points or tags), and an interconnected mesh of XBee's configured as routers, it is possible to bring real-time data from the endpoint (or tag) to your PC. In addition you can send messages to your sensors via the XBee network to reconfigure them, put some or all of them to sleep, or change parameters such as transmission or recording rate. 13948: The analysis of fish otoliths is increasingly incorporated into archaeological research. A study of archaeological otoliths (Argyrosomus japonicus, Macquaria ambigua, Pagrus auratus and Sillaginodes punctata) from an estuarine mound site in Greenfields, South Australia was undertaken. Through analysing these otoliths, valuable information concerning fish populations, Indigenous subsistence strategies and human impacts on the ecosystem can be gained. When compared with modern fish population information, these data can suggest changes encompassing pre- and post-settlement. Otolith weight was used to determine total fish length. The size of fish present in the archaeological record may be indicative of the fishing techniques that were employed by local Indigenous people, for example, spearing in shallow water usually results in the capture of larger specimens, as they are easier to hit, while gill nets capture a narrow size range of fish dependent on the net's mesh size. The estimated age of the fish at time of death was determined by counting the annuli; the edge annulus was also recorded as being translucent or opaque, as this information indicates the season during which the fish died. Age data were used to investigate changes in fish populations over time. When combined with fish size data, changes in fish growth rates can be examined. The season the fish died can reveal information about seasonal use of sites or resources. The findings contribute to a more in-depth picture of the pre-European population and environment of the Northern Adelaide plains, wetlands and estuaries.

13949: The significant threats facing the world's shark populations have generated research and management efforts. 13950: Audio lures have been used with some success to attract fish, including common carp (Cyprinus carpio), into areas where they can be harvested; however, little is known about how carp in New Zealand respond to such stimuli. Carp were responding to all frequencies within five days, but the fastest responses were observed by fish in the 400 Hz treatment. 13951: Common carp (Cyprinus carpio) are a highly invasive fish that are considered a pest in many of the countries where they have been introduced. Due to their abundance and wide distributions, controlling carp populations is logistically difficult, and there are a limited number of viable tools available to managers. Development of a toxic bait would be a logistically simple and inexpensive tool managers could use to reduce pest fish populations. Previous attempts to develop a toxic fish bait have met with limited success, probably due to poor uptake by carp and significant non-target by-catch. We present research on the development of a bait that floats, is structurally robust for long periods in water, and is highly palatable to carp with or without a toxin added. The baits we have developed consist of a high proportion of brewers spent grains (BSG). BSG is the main by-product of beer production and its disposal can create an environmental problem, yet it is high in nutritional value and a potential alternative protein source in feeds. Our experiments have identified the optimum bait formulation to meet the desired bait characteristics, and palatability experiments have shown that they are readily consumed by carp. Furthermore, additional flavours have been added to bait formulations to increase palatability and to also help mask the unpleasant taste of the toxin. To further increase bait acceptance, the toxin will be micro-encapsulated with palatable flavours and a surfactant to increase absorption rates across the intestine wall.

13955: The identification of genetic markers for high resolution population structure analysis can be both costly and labour-intensive. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies promise to confront this challenge. However, practical examples of their application for this purpose in non-model species are still rare. Here we present the methods and outcomes of an approach to combine SNP and microsatellite discovery in eastern Australian sea mullet (Mugil cephalus) using limited NGS. DNA was extracted from fins of sea mullet from three regions along the eastern Australian coastline (Townsville, south-east Queensland, and Newcastle). The samples were then used to prepare reduced genome representation libraries (RRLs) for each sampling region. Following considerations of expected sequencing output, estimated genome size, and the minimum number of individuals in the marker discovery panel, four principal steps were implemented to generate regional RRLs: (1) genome fragmentation using restriction enzymes EcoRI and MseI, (2) enrichment of EcoRI-cleaved DNA fragments, (3) selective amplifications, and (4) fragment size selections. 13958: Documenting the long-term effects of marine protected areas (MPAs) has been challenging due to a general lack of early data on the composition of reef fish communities inside and outside no-take areas. While we are starting to gain a strong appreciation for the effects of MPA zoning on high-diversity coral reef ecosystems within the Indo-Pacific (e.g. Philippines, Great Barrier Reef), we have a relatively poor understanding of the impact of MPA zoning on comparatively low-diversity Caribbean coral reef fish communities. Here we build upon an early study (1991-95) of the Saba Marine Park (MP) and provide an update on how the composition, abundance and biomass of target and non-target reef fish species have changed across take and no-take zones over the two decades since the Saba MP was established (1987). We explored the contrasting roles that natural variation and fishing pressure play in shaping change within the Saba MP reef fish community, and how trends within this low-diversity system compare with those found in long-term studies of similarly small-scale marine protected areas.

13959: Spencer Gulf represents an area of economic significance to the fisheries and aquaculture sectors of South Australia. The region is also experiencing considerable industrial growth and zoning for marine parks is underway. Given the level of proposed development it is imperative that the fisheries and aquaculture sectors have a better understanding of how future developments may impact their industries. We will provide a whole of Spencer Gulf ecosystem model to the fisheries and aquaculture sectors with the capability to address 'what if' scenarios. A suite of linked habitat, biophysical, trophodynamic and economic models will be developed that can be used to assess and optimize the future ecological and economic performance of the seafood industry in Spencer Gulf. Thus, managers will obtain sound, evidenced-based information on the impacts of current and future developments in Spencer Gulf. This project represents part of a broader initiative through Marine Innovations South Australia that also encompasses infrastructure and port development, as well as mining, energy, and other industrial interests.

13960: The Murray River estuary and Coorong form a system heavily regulated by a series of barrages, used to control freshwater flow from the Murray-Darling Basin. Water allocation upstream and droughts turned the system into a hypersaline environment, restricting the distribution and abundances of many species. During this period, the commercially valuable Yellow-eye mullet (Aldrichetta forsteri) remained highly abundant, likely attributed to their tolerance of a wide range of salinities, successful recruitment, decreased predation and their opportunistic feeding behaviour and omnivorous diet. A continuous water release since September 2010 has resulted in greatly reduced salinities and a redistribution of invertebrate and fish assemblages throughout the system. The aims of this study were to determine 1) the diet of A. forsteri in the Murray River estuary and Coorong after the barrage release, and 2) any differences in diet between two distinctive regions. Fish were collected in March 2012 at several locations within the Murray Estuary and North Lagoon using seine and gill nets. Over 170 mullet were caught, with juveniles being more abundant in the Murray Mouth and adults in the North Lagoon of the Coorong. Stable isotope analysis was used to determine diet in relation to food availability, while gut contents were analysed for a more detailed assessment of the recent diet composition. The results will be presented in light of their potential implications for the distribution of A. forsteri in the system as well as the species' adaptability to a changing estuarine environment.

13961: The shortfin mako (Isurus oxyrinchus) is an important component of pelagic shark community ranging through most tropical and temperate oceans of the world. In Chilean waters, is caught in commercial oceanic long-line and gill-net fisheries that target swordfishes, as well as in the artisanal longline fishery. This artisanal fishery is the only fishery that has sharks as target species, where in addition to I. oxyrinchus; this fishery has a bycatch of blue shark (Prionace glauca). During 2005 and 2010, 1241 I. oxyrinchus and 1153 P. glauca were collected in 178 longline sets off Caldera, Chile (c. 27°S, 70°W). Catch composition had a significant bias towards mako sharks in 2005, but was biased towards blue sharks in 2010. The predominance of the smaller size-classes in both years suggests a consistent behaviour, with I. oxyrinchus females using the coastal area where the fishery is conducted as pupping and possibly, a nursery zone during spring and summer. Considering the catch (or catch per effort unit) as an indirect proxy for abundance the habitat selection may be due prey availability, SST and primary production, as these factors benefits the development and growth of juvenile sharks and its preys. Conservation measures are needed urgently in Chile to regulate both the artisanal fishery and the bycatch from industrial fisheries, in order to establish a minimum catch-size for sharks, conservative fishing quotas and delimitation of fishing areas to prevent the continued removal of immature specimens that may affect negatively the reproductive stock I. oxyrinchus.

13962: Despite the importance of King George whiting to the commercial and recreational fishing sectors in Victoria and South Australia, there are many unanswered questions associated with the life-cycle and movement of this species. Despite significant efforts, King George whiting in spawning condition have rarely been recorded in Victorian waters; the only known significant spawning areas for the species are in South Australian coastal waters. Whiting larvae are known to have a protracted larval phase of 3-5 months before settling into shallow seagrass beds in bays and inlets. However, it is unclear whether the larvae that supply both the Victorian and South Australian populations begin their journey from the same place. It is possible that nursery areas along the coast of southern Australia are replenished by larvae that were spawned from a single spawning area; a scenario that would have profound implications for management. Uncertainties over spawning sources are a major impediment to ensuring that key adult spawning aggregations in coastal waters are afforded adequate protection from fishing. Here we describe the genetic techniques being employed to investigate the movement and connectivity of King George whiting in south-eastern Australian waters.

13963: The ACT government stocks and monitors four medium sized urban lakes (20-150 ha) in Canberra and monitors one other large lake (680 ha), stocked by NSW DII. Monitoring of fish communities in these lakes has been undertaken since the late 1970s using unweighted multifilament gill nets. Fish survey methods have inherent bias but with increasing animal welfare concerns about gill netting and increasing cost pressures there has been a widespread shift in community fish sampling towards using electrofishing. This study examines boat based electrofishing as a potential replacement for gill netting in the long term monitoring program. Results show that electrofishing catches as many, or more, species than gill nets however, caught ratios and the overall numbers of some species within a lake were different between the methods. The size structure of common species was found to be not significantly different between the two methods at a site or lake level. However, significant differences were also found between the numbers of some species such as Murray Cod collected between methods. Investigations into age, sex, and diet are often carried out on the urban lakes. Additional effort would be required to obtain similar sample sizes in an electrofishing survey as compared to gill nets for some species. Electrofishing was found to take less staff time and adequately surveyed an urban lake fish population and collect more species at a lake level. However, differences were found in size, species and ratio for some species in comparison to gill nets.

13964: Complementary methods of otolith element analysis (IRMS of stable isotopes and laser ablation ICP-MS of trace elements) were used to elucidate the stock structures in Western Australia of West Australian Dhufish Glaucosoma hebraicum and Snapper Pagrus auratus. Residency of adults during their most recent part of life and the existence of important nursery locations were investigated to evaluate the applicability of current spatial management. Stable oxygen isotope ratios (18O/16O), stable isotope composition (SI; δ18O, δ13C) and trace element composition (TE; 25Mg, 88Sr, 138Ba) in otolith margins indicated that adults were resident within each of four management areas in the West Coast Bioregion and, in the case of P. auratus, also at the broader scale of bioregions (Gascoyne, GCB; West, WCB; South, SCB). Data from otolith cores showed that G. hebraicum would have recruited by the early juvenile stage (<1 year old), to the management area where they will remain as adults. In contrast adult P. auratus in each bioregion or management area of the WCB would recruit from a range of nurseries. However, classification analyses demonstrated substantial self-recruitment within the WCB and SCB and within two of the four areas of the WCB. Adults of each species could be treated as separate stocks in each management area and/or bioregion. However, while recruitment of juvenile G. hebraicum to adult stocks would occur primarily from adjacent nurseries within areas of the WCB, adult P. auratus in any one bioregion and area within the WCB were derived from a range of nurseries, their importance requiring further investigation.

13966: Recent trends in freshwater ecology have seen an increase in the use of functional traits (characteristics of an organism that contribute to its fitness or performance) for ecological research as an alternative to traditional biotic indices. Functional traits are reportedly an informative currency of investigation because they are able to incorporate regional differences in species assemblages, are directly related to the habitat template, and can answer more general ecological questions including why fish live where they do, what is the range of diversity within an ecosystem, and why are some species naturally rare? This poster presentation outlines some preliminary exploration of the functional trait diversity and trait environment relationships for Australian freshwater fish. Results indicate that Australian species can be classified into three reproductive strategies resulting from adaptive responses to environmental conditions: periodic, opportunistic and equilibrium. These strategies optimize fitness within environmentally predictable, unpredictable and stable systems, respectively. Quantification of the degree of phylogenetic dependence constraining functional traits indicates that morphological traits are more evolutionarily labile than life history traits, and that phylogeny is important for shaping species traits at broad taxonomic scales whereas finer ecological processes are more important for shaping interspecific trait variation at lower taxonomic scales. This work forms an exploratory phase of my PhD and will be used to inform future field studies looking to quantify intraspecific variation in functional traits at local and regional scales.

13967: Adult female white sharks can reach 6m total length and exceed 2000kg. Although they can attain large sizes, the incidence of mature female white sharks larger than 4.8m at the Neptune Islands aggregation area is uncommon. In order to minimise the human impacts on white sharks, it is essential to understand the residency periods and site fidelity by individuals at important aggregation areas. Here we describe the seasonality and frequency of visitation of mature female white sharks to the Neptune Islands. An extensive photographic database for the period of January 2009 to February 2012 was developed. Mature females were observed to visit the area from late May to mid August (autumn-early winter), whereas mature males which were sighted year round. Of the mature females identified, 50% were resighted in annual, consecutive years throughout the study, in marked contrast to findings from populations in other parts of the world. The sexual segregation exhibited and the degree of connectivity between the South and North Neptune Island groups are described, as well as the potential implications for the management of the species in Australian waters.

13968: Northern Australia is a global stronghold for populations of euryhaline and coastal elasmobranchs, particularly rare, threatened, endangered and protected species, such as sawfishes and river sharks, including Pristis clavata, Pristis microdon, Pristis zijsron, Anoxypristis cuspidata, Glyphis garricki and Glyphis glyphis and also, the Freshwater Whipray Himantura dalyensis. These species, along with other sharks and rays are of major cultural, spiritual and totemic significance to the traditional, Indigenous coastal communities in northern Australia. While many of these species continue to be at risk, effective conservation and management is currently limited by an acute lack of data, particularly in the remote gulf rivers and inshore waters of the Northern Territory. Systematic monitoring of abundance and distribution, and also, improved understanding of biology, connectivity, habitat requirements, population genetic structure and key threats, are essential to inform population status, assessment and trajectories. In the intact, cultural landscapes of northern Australia, Indigenous ecological knowledge (and collaboration with remote Indigenous communities), also has the potential to provide invaluable knowledge and insights into population status, biology, movement and ecology. As part of the recently-funded, NERP Marine Biodiversity Hub, this PhD project will adopt an innovative, cross-cultural approach to improving knowledge and understanding of euryhaline elasmobranchs in the Roper River region, in the remote western Gulf of Carpentaria. Building on previous surveys and research, this project aims to improve understanding of biology, distribution, habitat utilisation and movement, through systematic monitoring, tagging, close-kin genetic analysis and tracking of priority species. The project will also, undertake cultural studies, surveys and interviews to document indigenous ecological knowledge of key species.

13969: Shark populations have experienced a dramatic worldwide decline due to overfishing, largely because they are targeted for their highly priced fins. Indonesia is the world's highest harvester of shark fins, and the Arafura Sea particularly is a region of intensive shark fishing activity. Recent population genetic studies found high connectivity among Indonesian and Australian shark populations. Furthermore, Indonesian fishermen often venture into protected areas within Australian waters. This has resulted in conflicts over shared marine resources. Little is known about catch composition of the Indonesian shark fisheries, particularly in the Arafura Sea, and whether sharks are systematically poached in Australian waters. During my PhD I am planning to address these knowledge gaps by: - Determining the catch composition of Indonesian shark fisheries in the Arafura Sea. This will be achieved by DNA barcoding samples of dried shark fins collected from GPS tracked fishing vessels, as well as local fish markets. - Investigating fine-scale population genetic structure in Western Australia, Northern Australia and Indonesia for one of the main coral-reef associated target species: the grey reef shark (C. amblyrhynchos), identifying possible conflicts among the two nations over shared marine resources. - Determining provenance (region, country) of grey reef shark fins sold in local Indonesian fish markets via genetic assignment tests, providing insight as to whether poaching in Australian waters is a common practice. This project will increase our knowledge of these ecological important apex predators, and further develop the application of molecular genetics to monitor fin trade.
13970: Characterisation of diet is of fundamental importance in understanding the role a species plays in an ecosystem. This study used stomach content (SCA) and stable isotope analyses (SIA) to explore inter- and intra- species resource partitioning for three sympatric resident ray species (Dasyatis fluviorum, Neotrygon kuhlii and Himantura toshi) in Moreton Bay, Queensland. Stomach content analysis suggests that all species feed on benthic organisms but with significant differences in proportions and occurrence of preferred prey items between and within species. Major prey groups for N. kuhlii, D. fluviorum and H. toshi were polychaetes, brachyuran crabs and carid shrimps, respectively; indicating that these three species are partitioning available resources. Ontogenetic shifts in dietary preference were also apparent in all species. Stable isotope analysis was conducted for 15N and 13C on prey items and elasmobranch muscle tissue to test the relationship between consumer and prey stable isotope values. The expected complementary nature of SCA and SIA will be explored in data presented. Given the caveats associated with bulk stable isotope analysis in elasmobranch studies, validation of bulk SIA is required in order for it to be used as an accurate dietary analysis tool. With the current state of elasmobranch populations worldwide, confidence in interpretation and reliability of results generated from non-destructive methods is imperative for future management and conservation strategies.

13971: Sharks play a key role in marine ecosystems and knowledge of their trophic ecology is critical to a better understanding of this role as well as their future management. This study investigated the gross conversion efficiency (GCE) of juvenile Port Jackson sharks, Heterodontus portusjacksoni, at various daily ration sizes. Sharks were obtained from the bycatch of a commercial fishery operating in the lower Hawkesbury River, N.S.W, Australia and kept under controlled laboratory conditions in recirculating aquaria. Sharks were measured, weighed and randomly assigned to groups, fed squid at four different ration sizes proportional to body weight (2%, 4%, 6% and 8% BW) for 21 days, as well as a starvation treatment (0% BW) for 7 days. Sharks were measured and weighed at the conclusion of these periods therefore allowing for calculations on Hepatosomatic Index (HSI), Condition Factor (CF), GCE and specific growth. The minimum maintenance ration was 2.32% BW day-1 and the maximum conversion efficiency was 34.36% at a ration level of 6.37% BW day-1. The starvation ration caused a significant loss of body weight and gross conversion efficiency decreased after the maximum level. However, the CF and HSI increased suggesting both an increase in body condition and energy storage in the liver. This study contributes to an understanding of elasmobranch trophic ecology, especially for benthic sharks.

13972:
The last decade has brought about a remarkable change in public awareness of the threat to sharks and the need for their protection. Two media trends have contributed significantly to this change: a) the advent of social media, including blogs and social networking, which re-post and propagate information; and b) the rise of shark conservation as entertainment through movies and television programmes such as 'Sharkwater' and Gordon Ramsey's 'Shark Bait'.

While these trends have undoubtedly mobilized public opinion, they have largely focused on banning the wasteful and distasteful practice of shark finning in many major fishing grounds, and in more recent years on the creation of shark "sanctuaries" mainly in the waters of small poor developing countries. The extent to which science has played a part in these conservation successes is limited. Campaigns have been aimed at politicians and public opinion, and have often either not had a strong scientific component or have made selective use of scientific information to support their cause. As one example, my estimate of the number of sharks killed for the shark fin trade has been widely mis-cited or exaggerated in favour of higher estimates for which I can find no clear scientific basis. In this case, while science is inevitably reduced to media sound bites, its underlying accuracy and defensibility is critical when designing effective conservation policies. For this reason, shark scientists must insist that standards such as independent peer review of results are maintained, and authors should speak up when conservation campaigns misrepresent findings.

Left behind in this era of media-friendly shark campaigns is the need for sustainable shark fisheries. Finning regulations do not prevent sharks from being threatened by overfishing and the creation of shark sanctuaries will not protect sharks if prohibitions on shark fishing are not enforced. Under the current lack of catch controls in many nations' coastal zones and on the high seas millions of sharks remain vulnerable to over-exploitation. In spite of this, shark scientists pursuing untelegenic topics such as ageing shark vertebrae, compiling and quality-checking fishing records, and constructing and running stock assessment models, cannot be blamed for feeling irrelevant to the work of shark conservation groups focused on finning and sanctuaries. It is not realistic to believe that all, or even most, sharks can be protected without fisheries management. Therefore, a scientific understanding of species' productivities, exploitation rates and recovery times will be critical to maintaining shark populations and marine ecosystems. We should all do more to acknowledge and support important shark research which will never feature on the Discovery Channel.

Although in some cases available science is not fully or effectively utilized by shark conservation campaigns, in many cases there are simply no scientific results to inform policy decision-making. This was, up until earlier this year, the situation for sharks in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean, but the first analyses of the longest-term and most comprehensive shark datasets held by any Regional Fisheries Management Organization (RFMO) was released by the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC) in August 2011. These analyses show consistent, dramatic declines in abundance and size of oceanic whitetip sharks in three independent data sets. Despite this undisputed evidence, and bans on retaining oceanic whitetip sharks in two of the five other tuna RFMOs, no member country has proposed any WCPFC management action for this species. This case points to a worrying de-coupling of shark science and shark conservation which prevents the kind of synergy needed to create political support for controls on shark fishing. When scientists and conservationists fail to coordinate their agendas, both sides, and most of all sharks, stand to lose critical opportunities for progress.

13973:
The European Union (EU) has been slow to regulate elasmobranch fishing and champion shark protection, but has taken significant steps toward conserving these species since 2006. The EU's notorious not-so-distant past – characterized by severe population depletion, unregulated fishing and exceptionally weak regulations – is now finally being balanced by increasing regulation of EU elasmobranch fisheries and growing interest in securing international shark protections.

EU fishery managers have shut down several unsustainable shark fisheries, established many new elasmobranch quotas, and fully protected several threatened species. These actions, however, came only after serious overfishing had already occurred. Moreover, there are still no limits for the current main targets of EU shark fisheries while many threatened species remain woefully under-protected. The lengthy process to close loopholes in the EU shark finning ban is finally in its final months, but the widely recommended prohibition on at-sea fin removal is by no means the certain outcome.

On the international front, the EU has had reasonable success promoting protection for particularly vulnerable shark species through Regional Fishery Management Organizations, even without protecting the same species at home. The EU, thanks to Germany and Belgium, has championed measures for porbeagle and spurdog through global wildlife treaties (the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species and the Convention on Migratory Species) with mixed results.

The 2009 EU Shark Action Plan, while long overdue, has set the stage for continuing policy improvements on all these fronts. The long-term sustainability of European shark populations depends on prompt and full implementation of this Plan by, among other things, closing finning ban loopholes, enforcing science-based fishing limits, and protecting endangered species. Given the EU's influence on international fisheries policies and developing countries, such progress is also key to a brighter future for elasmobranchs around the world.

This presentation will detail progress toward these achievements and outline, with recommendations, steps for securing the next significant milestones in EU elasmobranch conservation policy.

13974:
The intensive exploitation of shark populations in West Africa has resulted in the collapse of fisheries and loss of biodiversity. Hence the Sub-Regional Action Plan for conservation and sustainable management of shark populations (PSRA-Requins) launched a project in 2004 promoting a sustainable shark resource management strategy within the region of the Sub-Regional Fisheries Commission. The project aims to improve the understanding of elasmobranch distribution, biology, bycatch rates and landings, as well as social and cultural uses. This information is fundamental in the planning adequate conservation and management strategies.

The results presented here relate to shark exploitation, the distribution of species encountered in each country and their conservation status. The information was gathered through a thorough review of the literature, existing databases and scientific monitoring of shark landings.

This project enabled the development of a conservation and sustainable shark management strategy in the sub-region. The first phase of the project lasted four years and the knowledge gained lead to establishing the shark conservation status and the shark landings development in the countries across West Africa and to updating the Red List of the IUCN, with regards to elasmobranchs in West Africa.

13975: Given the rising global concerns about the status of elasmobranch fishes, the paucity of available information on elasmobranchs in the Red Sea is worrisome. Research on stock assessment, population ecology and life history aspects are almost completely missing and it is suggested that even species estimates are far from being complete. This lack of data is critically hampering the development of any meaningful conservation efforts, such as the implementation of management initiatives to regulate the exploitation of Red Sea elasmobranch stocks. A new research project based in Saudi Arabia has been initiated to create a baseline of Red Sea shark populations as well as to provide scientific information to support new management plans. As part of an integrated approach, a range of fisheries dependent (market surveys) and independent (long-line and baited remote underwater video surveys (BRUVS)) shark population assessment methods are being implemented throughout the Red Sea. Preliminary data indicate an alarming scarcity of elasmobranch species in Saudi Arabian waters in concert with increasingly high catch levels, pointing to currently unsustainable levels of fishing in this area. The project will further involve the assimilation of data from elasmobranch tagging studies, genetic analyses and the assessment of potential nursery areas. Collectively the study aims to establish a baseline foundation for future studies on Red Sea elasmobranchs.

13976: In April 2009 the EU council of fisheries ministers adopted the Community Plan of Action for Sharks (CPoA). 13977:
As pressures on the marine environment increase, novel approaches to conservation are required. It's estimated that at least 33 million sharks are killed annually both in targeted fisheries, and as bycatch. Many chondrichthyan species are apex predators and their rapid removal is impacting entire ecosystems. The combination of lack of knowledge, poor management and high fisheries mortality increases the potential loss of phylogenetic diversity.

The EDGE of Existence Programme aims to conserve Evolutionarily Distinct (ED) and Globally Endangered (GE) (EDGE) species, thus helping to maintain the focal taxon's diversity, and maximise their ability to adapt and survive anthropogenic and environmental challenges. Applying the EDGE criteria yields different focal species when compared to 'classical' conservation drivers, such as habitat degradation. EDGE Mammals, and Amphibians, projects are already established and EDGE Aquatics is now progressing; in the first instance it will address Sharks, as well as Corals Reefs.

EDGE species are identified using available phylogenetic data to assess 'ED' - the absence of a complete phylogeny, sequence data are being analysed to determine focal chondrichthyes - and the IUCN Red List for 'GE'; with the combined 'EDGE' scores providing a priority list.

The EDGE programme not only approaches conservation from a new perspective, it is focussed on long-term community lead initiatives in developing nations. These species rarely have existing conservation attention and in-country 'EDGE Fellows' are trained to develop projects to benefit each one, as well as build local capacity in regions where the effects of marine pressures is greatest.
13978:
Data collected at landing sites across the United Arab Emirates (UAE) indicate that shark catches are increasingly high which suggests unsustainable levels of fishing. Research on the shark fishery is sparse and shark species occurring in the Arabian/Persian Gulf have not been comprehensively described. Furthermore, it is believed that the UAE is serving as a regional hub for the export and trade in shark fins and shark products to Asia.

Interviews conducted with fishermen across the country have suggested a recent large decline in shark abundance in UAE waters in parallel with the growth of targeted shark fishery. Market surveys are on-going with over 12,000 specimens already examined and genetic samples collected from a confirmed 28 species of sharks originating from UAE Gulf waters. Commercially important species include the milk shark Rhizoprionodon acutus, and the spottail shark, Carcharhinus sorrah, while other elasmobranchs such as the giant guitarfish, Rhinchobatus djiddensis, are most valued for their fins.

The Sultanate of Oman and Islamic Republic of Iran are the largest contributors to the trade in shark fins and shark products being processed in the UAE for export to various countries around the world. Further data collected includes information on the fishery characteristics, species composition, seasonal abundance, distribution, genetics and fin trade of sharks. This data lays the foundations for future studies on sharks in the region as well as provides scientific information to support the development and implementation of new national and regional regulations on the exploitation of these stocks and their conservation.
